milestone.title: Apple launches the Macintosh
milestone.note: The January 24 debut put a mass-market graphical desktop, icons, windows, mouse control, and consistent application design at the center of personal computing's future.

editorNote: Extra Edition: Apple has placed the mouse, windows and pictures at the center of a $2,495 personal computer—and challenged the rest of the industry to follow.
morningLine: Cupertino opens a new window on personal computing while Atari regroups and home-computer shelves keep moving.

lead.headline: Macintosh Arrives: Apple Bets $2,495 on the Mouse
lead.dek: The compact 128K machine brings Lisa-style windows, icons and graphics to a far wider market—and seeks a place beside the Apple II and IBM PC.
body: CUPERTINO, Calif.—Apple Computer unveiled the Macintosh on January 24, placing a mouse-controlled graphical desktop inside a compact 20-pound machine carrying a suggested retail price of $2,495. Apple chairman Steven P. Jobs declared that the company expected Macintosh to become a third industry standard alongside the Apple II and IBM PC.

The specifications make the wager concrete: 128KB of memory, 64KB of read-only memory, a crisp black-and-white screen, one 3.5-inch disk drive, two serial ports, an external-drive connection and built-in sound. Menus, icons and overlapping windows replace much command-line ritual, while cut and paste lets words and pictures travel between documents.

For its first 100 days, Macintosh buyers receive MacWrite and MacPaint without extra charge. MacWrite mixes typefaces, sizes and illustrations; MacPaint supplies brushes, patterns, shapes and erasers. Microsoft Multiplan is available immediately, Lotus has promised a Macintosh version of 1-2-3, and Apple says more than 100 outside companies are developing products.

The polish comes with limits. Macintosh runs one major application at a time, and a contemporary test found that changing programs to move a picture into a letter could take 20 to 30 seconds. Its 128K memory and single internal drive leave little room to spare, even as the interface makes the computer feel unusually approachable.

Apple is backing the launch with a $15 million, 100-day advertising drive following Ridley Scott's nationally aired “1984” commercial during the January 22 Super Bowl. A Fremont factory is prepared to turn out one Macintosh every 27 seconds; now dealers, universities, offices and home users will decide whether Apple's new desktop language becomes computing's next vernacular.

stories.headline: Lisa 2 Family Cuts the Price of Apple’s Workstation
body: Apple also introduced three Lisa 2 configurations priced from roughly $3,500 to $5,500—far below the original Lisa's near-$10,000 ticket. The machines offer more storage and power than Macintosh and can keep several applications running at once.

The shared 3.5-inch disk format and planned software connections make Lisa 2 the senior member of a family rather than a solitary executive machine. Jobs conceded that the first Lisa suffered from high price, thin software support and an overly narrow Fortune 500 sales focus.

stories.headline: MacWrite and MacPaint Lead the Software Parade
body: Apple's two bundled programs are more than demonstrations: they define the new machine's point-and-click vocabulary. MacWrite combines varied fonts with search, replacement and pasted illustrations; MacPaint turns the mouse into a pencil, brush, eraser and geometric drafting tool.

Apple expects independent publishers to supply about 90 percent of Macintosh software and forecasts at least 500 packages by year's end. Microsoft, Lotus and Software Publishing Corporation are among the named supporters, while Apple's coming MacTerminal is meant to connect the compact machine to larger systems.

stories.headline: Atari Reorders the Front Office as the Game Crash Bites
body: Atari realigned management on January 24 as James Morgan continued the difficult work of stabilizing Warner Communications' battered games subsidiary. The change follows steep 1983 reversals and extensive layoffs amid the contraction of the American console market.

The home-computer side remains active despite the corporate strain. Period catalogs show games, disk drives, printer gear and utilities still arriving for the Atari 400/800 and XL audience—a busy shelf beneath a company fighting to restore order above it.

stories.headline: Satellite Television Aims Straight at the Home
body: The nation's first direct-to-home satellite television service is preparing to begin operation, UPI reported January 25. The plan promises pictures delivered from orbit without depending on a local broadcaster or a neighborhood cable plant.

Receiving equipment and economics will determine how broadly the experiment travels, but the debut marks home satellite reception as one of consumer electronics' most forward-looking distribution bets.
